title: Expressivism and the Meaning of 'Good'
subtitle: Is calling something good describing it, or cheering for it?
objectives: By the end you will be able to state Moore's open question argument and explain what it was meant to show and why it remains contested.
By the end you will be able to explain emotivism and its successors (prescriptivism and modern expressivism) and how they differ.
By the end you will be able to describe Blackburn's quasi-realist program and what it means to 'earn the right' to talk of moral truth.
By the end you will be able to set out the Frege-Geach problem with a worked example and assess the main expressivist replies.
hook:
Here are two sentences: "This knife is sharp" and "This knife is good." They look grammatically identical. Both seem to attribute a property to the knife. But try to say what property "good" names. Sharpness you can test with a tomato. Goodness? A good knife is sharp; a good argument is valid; a good person is kind; a good night's sleep is long and deep. The word seems to do something other than describe.

Last lesson we asked whether there are moral facts. This lesson approaches the question from the side of language. What does "good" *mean*? On one answer, developed through the twentieth century, moral words do not describe the world at all. They express our attitudes toward it: approval, disapproval, commitment. This view, now called **expressivism**, promises to explain everything distinctive about moral talk without the "queer" facts that troubled Mackie. Whether it can also explain moral *reasoning* is one of the great puzzles of modern philosophy.

sections.heading: Moore's Open Question Argument
sections.body:
The story begins in Cambridge with G. E. Moore's *Principia Ethica* (1903). Moore asked what "good" means, and gave a famously deflating answer: "good is good, and that is the end of the matter." Goodness, he argued, is a **simple, indefinable** property, like yellow. You cannot explain yellow to someone who has never seen it by listing its parts; you can only point. Likewise, goodness cannot be broken down into anything else.

His argument for this is the **open question argument**. Take any proposed definition of good in natural terms, say "good means pleasant" (Bentham's hedonism, Day 61) or "good means what we desire to desire." Now ask: "This is pleasant, but is it good?" That question is **open**: a competent speaker can sensibly wonder about it. Compare: "This man is a bachelor, but is he unmarried?" That question is **closed**: anyone who understands the words knows the answer. If "good" just meant "pleasant," the first question would be as closed as the second. It is not, so "good" does not mean "pleasant," and the same test defeats every other natural definition.

Moore called the mistake of identifying goodness with a natural property the **naturalistic fallacy**. (Strictly, it is not a fallacy of reasoning but an alleged false identification.) It echoes Hume's point (Day 50) that you cannot validly derive an "ought" from an "is" alone. Moore concluded that goodness is a **non-natural** property, known by **intuition**, which made him the founder of twentieth-century non-naturalist realism.

The argument has well-known weaknesses:
- **The paradox of analysis.** If every correct analysis must be obvious, then no analysis could ever be informative. But some correct definitions are surprising: it took mathematicians centuries to define "continuous function" correctly.
- **A posteriori identity.** Water turned out to be H₂O, yet "This is water, but is it H₂O?" was an open question for most of history. (If you took the Logic track, this is Kripke's necessary a posteriori from Lesson 4.) So the openness of "Is pleasure good?" may show only that the identity is not obvious from meaning, not that it is false. This is exactly the reply naturalist realists like the Cornell realists made.

Yet the argument still nags. Whatever natural property we offer, the question "but is it good?" seems to retain a special kind of openness, a practical one: it asks whether to *favor* the thing. That observation would be put to a very different use.

sections.heading: Emotivism: Boo and Hurrah
sections.body:
In the 1930s the logical positivists (Day 71) held that a meaningful statement must be either true by definition or verifiable by experience. Moral statements are neither. A. J. Ayer, in *Language, Truth and Logic* (1936), drew the bold conclusion: moral judgments are not statements at all. In a well-known passage he says that if I tell someone "You acted wrongly in stealing that money," I am not stating anything more than if I had simply said "You stole that money." The word "wrongly" adds no fact; it adds a tone of disapproval, as if I had said the sentence with a special tone of horror or added exclamation marks.

This view, **emotivism**, was soon nicknamed the "boo-hurrah theory": "Stealing is wrong" means roughly "Stealing, boo!" and "Generosity is good" means "Generosity, hurrah!"

Notice how neatly it handles Moore's open question. Of course "This is pleasant, but is it good?" is open: the first half describes, while the second asks whether to cheer. No description could ever settle a question about attitude. Emotivism also explains the link between moral judgment and motivation (if you sincerely judge something wrong, you tend to be moved against it, because the judgment *is* an attitude), and it dissolves the queerness worry: there are no strange moral facts because moral words were never in the business of stating facts.

Charles Stevenson (*Ethics and Language*, 1944) refined the view. Moral language, he said, has **emotive meaning**: it expresses attitudes and tries to influence others' attitudes. "This is good" works something like "I approve of this; do so as well." Moral disagreement is then a **disagreement in attitude**, like two friends who disagree about where to eat, rather than a disagreement in belief.

The obvious objection is that emotivism seems to make ethics irrational. If moral claims are expressions of feeling, how can there be good and bad moral arguments? Isn't it then just a contest of manipulation? Stevenson accepted that moral persuasion could be non-rational, which many found alarming.

R. M. Hare (*The Language of Morals*, 1952) tried to restore reason to the picture. On his **prescriptivism**, moral judgments are not expressions of feeling but **universal prescriptions**, akin to commands that apply to everyone in relevantly similar circumstances. Their logic is real: if I prescribe that you should not lie to me, then, by **universalizability**, I must accept the same prescription for myself in your position. Hare used this to argue his way, in later work, to a form of utilitarianism.

sections.heading: Quasi-Realism: Earning the Right to Truth
sections.body:
Modern **expressivism** is the descendant of these views. Its central claim is about the *function* of moral language: to judge that lying is wrong is to be in a conative state (a state of planning, preferring or disapproving) rather than a belief representing a moral fact. Its leading defenders are Simon Blackburn (*Spreading the Mind*, 1984; *Ruling Passions*, 1998) and Allan Gibbard (*Wise Choices, Apt Feelings*, 1990; *Thinking How to Live*, 2003). Gibbard treats moral judgment as the acceptance of norms or, later, as **planning**: deciding what to do in all sorts of circumstances, including hypothetical ones.

Blackburn's distinctive contribution is **quasi-realism**. The crude emotivist says, in effect, "Moral claims aren't really true or false." That clashes with ordinary practice: we say "It's true that cruelty is wrong," "I believe that's unjust," "I was mistaken about that." Blackburn's project is to show that an expressivist can **earn the right** to all this realist-sounding talk.

The key tool is **minimalism about truth**. Saying "It is true that cruelty is wrong" adds nothing to saying "Cruelty is wrong," in the spirit of the T-schema (Logic track, Lesson 5). So if expressivism can explain what "cruelty is wrong" does, it can explain "it is true that cruelty is wrong" for free. Similarly, calling a moral view a "belief" just marks it as a settled commitment you are prepared to defend.

Take the strongest objection to subjectivism: **mind-dependence**. Surely expressivism implies that if we had approved of kicking dogs, kicking dogs would have been fine? Blackburn replies no. The sentence "If we had approved of kicking dogs, it would still have been wrong" is itself a moral claim, and it expresses an attitude we actually hold: our disapproval is directed at the dog's pain, not at our own feelings. The quasi-realist can therefore affirm, sincerely and in the same breath, that cruelty is wrong regardless of what anyone thinks. What he denies is that this is a deep metaphysical report rather than a moral stance.

This leads to a striking situation. The sophisticated quasi-realist and the quietist realist from the end of last lesson may say all the same sentences. Some philosophers call this the **problem of creeping minimalism**: if expressivists can say everything realists say, what, if anything, does their disagreement consist in?

sections.heading: The Frege-Geach Problem
sections.body:
The deepest challenge to expressivism comes from logic. Gottlob Frege (Day 69) had noted that a sentence can occur in a larger sentence without being asserted. Peter Geach, in papers in 1960 and 1965 ("Assertion"), turned this observation into an argument; John Searle raised a similar point in 1962. It is now called the **Frege-Geach problem** or the **embedding problem**.

Consider this argument:
1. Lying is wrong.
2. If lying is wrong, then getting your little brother to lie is wrong.
3. Therefore, getting your little brother to lie is wrong.

This is a valid case of modus ponens (Logic track, Lesson 1). Validity requires that "lying is wrong" mean the *same thing* in premise 1 and in the antecedent of premise 2; otherwise we would have the fallacy of equivocation.

But look at what the expressivist says. In premise 1, "Lying is wrong" expresses disapproval of lying. In premise 2, though, the speaker expresses no disapproval of lying at all; someone who thinks lying is fine can accept premise 2, since it merely says *if* lying is wrong, something follows. So in premise 2 the phrase cannot be functioning as an expression of disapproval. If its meaning is its expressive function, it means something different in the two premises, and the argument equivocates. Yet it is obviously valid.

The problem generalizes to every **unasserted context**: negations ("Lying is not wrong"), questions ("Is lying wrong?"), disjunctions, and attitude reports ("She wonders whether lying is wrong"). A descriptive theory explains them all at once: the content "lying is wrong" is a proposition, which can be asserted, negated, supposed or questioned. Expressivism must build a whole semantics from attitudes instead.

**Blackburn's first reply** (1984) treated the conditional as expressing a **higher-order attitude**: approval of combining disapproval of lying with disapproval of getting others to lie. Someone who accepts the premises and rejects the conclusion has a "fractured sensibility" that clashes with itself. Critics, notably Bob Hale and Crispin Wright, objected that this makes the failing a moral one, a kind of inconsistency of taste, whereas the person who rejects the conclusion of a valid argument is guilty of a *logical* error.

**Later replies** treat the logic as arising from the inconsistency of the underlying states themselves, much as it is inconsistent to plan to go out and plan to stay in. Gibbard developed this with his planning states. Mark Schroeder's *Being For* (2008) showed how hard the details are: even explaining why "Lying is wrong" and "Lying is not wrong" are inconsistent requires care, since "not disapproving of lying" and "disapproving of not lying" are different states (this is the **negation problem**, raised by Nicholas Unwin in 1999). Schroeder concluded that expressivism can solve the problem only by taking on heavy commitments.

The debate remains open. Expressivists have made real progress, and the program has spread to other areas, such as expressivist theories of epistemic modals ("might") and of logic itself. But Frege-Geach remains the test that any expressivism must pass.

keyQuote.text: If I am asked 'What is good?' my answer is that good is good, and that is the end of the matter.
keyQuote.source: G. E. Moore, Principia Ethica (1903), section 6

modernConnection.title: Likes, Ratios and the Emotive Internet
modernConnection.body:
Social media sometimes looks like emotivism built into software. A "like," a heart, an angry-face reaction or a reposted call to boycott expresses an attitude and invites others to share it. Stevenson's account of moral language as expressing approval and trying to spread it reads almost like a description of how outrage travels online. A 2017 study led by William Brady, analyzing hundreds of thousands of tweets on contested topics such as gun control and same-sex marriage, found that each additional moral-emotional word (words such as "shame," "evil" or "disgust") was associated with a substantial increase in retweets, especially within like-minded networks.

Moral psychology adds a related claim. Jonathan Haidt's "social intuitionist" model (2001) proposed that most moral judgments are produced by fast intuitions and emotions, with reasoning usually arriving afterward to justify them, like a lawyer defending a client. That looks like empirical support for the emotivist picture, and Haidt explicitly cited Hume (Day 50), who wrote that morality is more properly felt than judged.

But be careful about what this shows. Expressivism is a theory of the *meaning* of moral words, not a claim that moral thinking is quick, emotional or unreflective. Blackburn and Gibbard insist that attitudes can be refined, criticized and made consistent, and the Frege-Geach debate is precisely about how moral *reasoning* works. Likewise, the psychological finding that emotion drives judgment does not settle whether there are moral facts; perceptions are also fast and automatic, yet they track real objects.

The online lesson may run the other way. The expressivist view highlights that moral talk is a tool for coordinating attitudes, which makes it powerful and dangerous. The question it presses on us is not whether our moral reactions are feelings, but whether they are the feelings we would endorse after reflection, and whether the platforms we use reward that reflection or bypass it.

vocabulary.definition: Moore's argument that for any natural property N, 'This is N, but is it good?' remains a meaningful question, so 'good' cannot mean N.
vocabulary.example: The open question argument says 'It maximizes happiness, but is it good?' is not a confused question.

vocabulary.definition: Moore's name for the alleged mistake of identifying goodness with a natural property such as pleasure.
vocabulary.example: Moore accused Bentham of the naturalistic fallacy for defining good as pleasure.

vocabulary.definition: The view, associated with Ayer and Stevenson, that moral judgments express emotions or attitudes rather than state facts.
vocabulary.example: For an emotivist, 'Cheating is wrong' works like 'Cheating, boo!'

vocabulary.definition: R. M. Hare's view that moral judgments are universalizable prescriptions, similar to commands that apply to everyone in relevantly similar situations.
vocabulary.example: On prescriptivism, saying 'You ought to keep promises' commits you to keeping your own.

vocabulary.definition: The modern view that moral judgments express non-representational states such as attitudes or plans, explained in terms of the function of moral language.
vocabulary.example: An expressivist holds that judging cruelty wrong is a stance against cruelty, not a perception of a moral fact.

vocabulary.definition: Simon Blackburn's program of showing that an expressivist can legitimately use realist-sounding talk of moral truth, belief and mistake.
vocabulary.example: A quasi-realist will say 'It's true that slavery was wrong, and would have been wrong even if everyone approved.'

vocabulary.definition: The challenge of explaining how moral sentences keep the same meaning in unasserted contexts such as conditionals, so that moral arguments can be valid.
vocabulary.example: The Frege-Geach problem asks what 'lying is wrong' means in 'If lying is wrong, then...'

vocabulary.definition: The view that saying a claim is true adds nothing substantial beyond asserting the claim itself.
vocabulary.example: By minimalism, 'It's true that kindness is good' says no more than 'Kindness is good.'

thinkingExercise.title: Test the Theories on Your Own Words
thinkingExercise.prompt: Examine how you actually use moral words, and see which theory fits best.
steps: Write three sentences you have recently said or thought using 'good', 'wrong' or 'should' about another person's action.
For each, write an emotivist paraphrase ('X, boo!'), a prescriptivist paraphrase (a universal command), and a realist paraphrase (a claim about a moral fact). Which paraphrase loses the least?
Apply Moore's open question test: pick a natural property you think is closely tied to goodness (happiness, fairness, flourishing) and ask whether 'It is N, but is it good?' feels open to you.
Build a short valid moral argument with a conditional premise. Explain, in your own words, why an expressivist must say something special about the conditional.
Decide: does the fact that moral sentences behave logically like descriptions count strongly against expressivism, or can the quasi-realist explain it away?

summary: Moore's open question argument claims no natural definition of 'good' is correct, since 'N, but is it good?' always remains open; critics cite the paradox of analysis and a posteriori identities like water = H₂O.
Emotivism (Ayer, Stevenson) says moral judgments express and seek to spread attitudes; Hare's prescriptivism treats them as universal prescriptions with genuine logic.
Modern expressivism (Blackburn, Gibbard) explains moral judgments as conative states such as disapproval or plans, which explains their motivating force without queer facts.
Blackburn's quasi-realism aims to earn the right to talk of moral truth and mind-independence, using minimalism about truth, which raises the question of what then separates it from realism.

The Frege-Geach problem asks how moral words keep their meaning in unasserted contexts like conditionals; expressivists have proposed higher-order attitudes and inconsistency of planning states, but the problem remains the central test.

quiz.question: According to Moore's open question argument, why can't 'good' mean 'pleasant'?
options: Because pleasure is sometimes bad
Because 'It is pleasant, but is it good?' is a meaningful, open question
Because pleasure cannot be measured
Because Hume proved it
quiz.explanation: If 'good' meant 'pleasant', the question would be as closed as 'Is this bachelor unmarried?' Its openness suggests the meanings differ.

quiz.question: Which reply to the open question argument appeals to the case of water and H₂O?
options: Two terms can pick out the same property even when their identity is not obvious from meaning
Water is not really H₂O
All identities are known a priori
Moral terms are meaningless
quiz.explanation: 'Is water H₂O?' was once an open question, yet water is H₂O. So openness may not show that goodness differs from a natural property.

quiz.question: On Ayer's emotivism, 'You acted wrongly in stealing that money' states the fact that you stole the money plus a further moral fact.
quiz.explanation: Ayer held that 'wrongly' adds no further fact; it only expresses the speaker's disapproval.

quiz.question: R. M. Hare's prescriptivism differs from emotivism chiefly by holding that moral judgments:
options: Describe natural facts
Are meaningless
Are universalizable prescriptions with their own logic
Are reports of the speaker's feelings
quiz.explanation: Hare treated moral judgments as universal prescriptions, so that consistency and universalizability give moral reasoning genuine rational constraints.

quiz.question: A quasi-realist says, 'Kicking dogs would be wrong even if everyone approved of it.' How does Blackburn make sense of this?
options: He claims moral facts exist in a Platonic realm
He admits this is a mistake on his view
He says the sentence is meaningless
He treats it as expressing our actual attitude, which is directed at the dog's suffering, not at our feelings
quiz.explanation: The counterfactual is itself a moral claim expressing our real disapproval of cruelty, which does not depend on anyone's approval.

quiz.question: The Frege-Geach problem arises because moral sentences appear in contexts, such as the antecedent of a conditional, where they are not being asserted.
quiz.explanation: In 'If lying is wrong, then...', no disapproval of lying is expressed, so the expressivist must explain why the phrase means the same as when asserted.

quiz.question: Critics such as Hale objected that Blackburn's 'higher-order attitude' solution to Frege-Geach fails because:
options: It makes the error in rejecting the conclusion a moral failing rather than a logical one
It relies on non-natural facts
It denies that modus ponens is valid
It was refuted by Moore
quiz.explanation: A person who accepts the premises and rejects the conclusion seems guilty of a logical mistake, not just a 'fractured sensibility'.

quiz.question: Minimalism about truth holds that 'It is true that cruelty is wrong' says nothing more than 'Cruelty is wrong.'
quiz.explanation: This is how the quasi-realist earns the right to call moral claims true without positing moral facts.

quiz.question: A study finds that posts with words like 'shameful' and 'evil' spread faster online. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Expressivism is proven true
Moral realism is refuted
Moral language has a powerful attitude-spreading function, as Stevenson stressed, though this does not settle what moral words mean
Moral words have no emotive meaning
quiz.explanation: The finding fits Stevenson's emphasis on emotive meaning, but metaethical theories concern meaning and truth, which psychological data alone cannot decide.

goDeeper.body:
Recent metaethics has produced **hybrid** theories that try to keep the advantages of both camps. Michael Ridge's **ecumenical expressivism** (*Impassioned Belief*, 2014) holds that a moral judgment is a combination of a belief and a non-cognitive state. Saying "Lying is wrong" expresses a belief that lying is forbidden by standards of a certain kind together with approval of those standards. Since a belief component is present, embedding is easier to handle; since an attitude component is present, the link to motivation is preserved. Critics ask whether such hybrids inherit the problems of both parents.

A related idea comes from the theory of **slurs** and of words like "oops" and "alas." Linguists such as Christopher Potts distinguish what a sentence says (its at-issue content) from what it conveys as a side comment (expressive content). "That damn dog is barking" says the dog is barking and expresses annoyance; the annoyance does not get negated in "That damn dog isn't barking." Some philosophers suggest moral terms might work similarly, but the analogy is imperfect: "It's not wrong to lie" really does deny that lying is wrong, whereas the expressive content of "damn" survives negation.

Finally, expressivism has spread far beyond ethics. Gibbard and others have offered expressivist accounts of epistemic normativity ("you ought to believe the evidence"), of probability and "might," and even of mathematical and logical claims. Huw Price calls this broader program **global expressivism**, asking whether all of language should be explained by what it does for speakers rather than by what it represents. If so, the realism debate might change shape entirely.

questions: If you can say 'cruelty would be wrong even if we approved of it' as a quasi-realist, what remains of the disagreement with realism?
Can there be a logic of attitudes and plans that is as rigorous as the logic of beliefs?
Does the open question argument apply equally to supernatural definitions, such as 'good means commanded by God'?
